name: Bertrand's paradox
seoTitle: Bertrand's paradox Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Bertrand's paradox: work out your result from the chances. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The Bertrand's paradox calculator is a free, no-sign-up statistics tool. Fill in the 13 fields it asks for and it works out the answer straight away, with the formula shown underneath.

Think of it as a shortcut for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Bertrand's paradox calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bertrand's paradox calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method of sampling, the chance and the chances); then you type in the chances (4), the chances (5), the chances (6) and number of random chords.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bertrand's paradox calculator
sections.html:
This one is not a single closed-form equation. It is driven by a page script that applies a set of rules — lookups, cut-offs and conditional branches — and the numbers you see are the script's output rather than the rearrangement of one line of algebra. The rules are what make the tool useful: a plain formula cannot express a table of thresholds or a choice between cases.

Practically, that means you can trust the result but cannot reproduce it with a pocket calculator. If you need to show your working, quote the inputs and the output rather than an equation.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bertrand's paradox calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the chances — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bertrand's paradox calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the chances, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter chances (4) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Chances (4) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (9 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Bertrand's paradox calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
